Guideline:
Abnormal Uterine Bleeding (AUB)

Definitions:
Abnormal Uterine Bleeding (AUB): Uterine bleeding that is abnormal in frequency, duration, regularity, or volume in a
nonpregnant individual of reproductive age.

AUB patterns:
§ Heavy Menstrual Bleeding (HMB): Excessive bleeding that interferes with quality of life or results in anemia.
§ Intermenstrual Bleeding (IMP): Bleeding between otherwise regular menstrual cycles.
§ Prolonged Menstrual Bleeding: Bleeding lasting >7 days in a single cycle.
§ Irregular Bleeding: Inconsistent cycle length (>20 days variation cycle to cycle).
§ Frequent Menstruation: Menstrual bleeding occurring more often than every 21 days.
§ Infrequent Menstruation: Bleeding occurring at intervals >35 days but <6 months (oligomenorrhea).
§ Spotting: Minimal bleeding that does not fulfill criteria for IMB or HMB.
§ Postcoital Bleeding (PCB): Bleeding following sexual intercourse; may coexist with AUB but also suggests lower
genital tract pathology.

PALM–COEIN categories:
§ Polyp.
§ Adenomyosis.
§ Leiomyoma.
§ Malignancy & Hyperplasia.
§ Coagulopathy.
§ Ovulatory dysfunction.
§ Endomterial origin.
§ Iatrogenic.
§ Not yet classified.


Scope:
This guideline applies to the diagnostic evaluation of patients presenting with:
• Heavy menstrual bleeding.
• Intermenstrual bleeding.
• Irregular or prolonged menstrual bleeding.
• Frequent or infrequent menstrual cycles.
• Postcoital bleeding suspected to originate from the uterus.
• Persistent unexplained uterine bleeding.

This guideline does NOT cover:
• Bleeding during confirmed pregnancy (miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy, gestational trophoblastic disease).
• Purely cervical or vaginal bleeding unrelated to uterine origin.
• Postmenopausal bleeding pathways.
• Management/treatment protocols.
• Obstetric hemorrhage.
• Known gynecologic malignancy surveillance.

Policy:
Requirements for coverage:

Documentation requirements:
• Life stage: adolescent / reproductive age / peri- or postmenopause.
• Bleeding pattern: as per above definitions.
• PALM–COEIN working category (at least “suspected structural vs non-structural”).


Coverage criteria - Laboratory testing:
In all reproductive-age females pregnancy test is mandatory.
Investigations should be directed by the clinical suspecion based on the FIGO-PALM-COEIN categories.

Baseline laboratory testing: (Approve at first visit)
In patients without a known hemostatic disorder:
• CBC.
• Ferritin.
• Pregnancy test.

Conditional tests:
• TSH (when endocrine or ovulatory dysfunction is suspected).
• LH, FSH, prolactin (when anovulation, pituitary-ovarian dysfunction, galactorrhea, or endocrine disorder is
suspected).
• Calculated free testosterone, calculated bioavailable testosterone, or free androgen index (If PCOS suspected
and labs required for Rotterdam criteria).
• PT, aPTT, Fibrinogen +/- VWD and hematology consultation (if heavy bleeding + any of the following):
§ Heavy menstrual bleeding since menarche.
§ ≥1 of: postpartum hemorrhage, surgery-related bleeding, bleeding associated with dental work.
§ ≥2 of the following symptoms: bruising 1-2 times/month, epistaxis 1-2 times/month, frequent gum bleeding,
family history of bleeding symptoms.

Coverage criteria - Imaging:
1) TVUS if any of the following:
• Structural cause suspected.
• Abnormal pelvic exam.
• Persistent or recurrent AUB.
• Suspected fibroid, polyp, adenomyosis, endometrial thickening.

2) Color flow Doppler can be added to TVUS for the following conditions:
1. Distinguishing adenomyosis vs fibroids.
2. Differentiating polyps vs submucosal leiomyoma.
3. Suspected uterine AV malformation.

3) Saline infusion sonography (SIS) can be added to TVUS for the following conditions:
1. Intracavitary lesion suspected.
2. TVUS nondiagnostic.
3. Need to better define polyp or submucosal myoma.

4) MRI pelvis approved if any of the following:
• Adenomyosis vs leiomyoma remains unclear.
• Mapping submucosal myoma extent.
• Complex anatomy before intervention.

*Hysterosalpingogram (HSG) is not routine for AUB workup.


Coverage criteria - Office-based procedures:
1) Endometrial biopsy for the following indications:
1. Age ≥45 years old.
2. Age <45 years old as below:
§ Any abnormal uterine bleeding in patients with BMI ≥30 kg/m2.
§ In patients with BMI <30 kg/m2, abnormal uterine bleeding that is persistent and occurs in the setting of one
of the following: chronic ovulatory dysfunction, other exposure to estrogen unopposed by progesterone,
failed medical management of the bleeding, or patients at high risk of endometrial cancer (eg, Lynch
syndrome, Cowden syndrome).
§ Premenopausal women who are anovulatory and have prolonged periods of amenorrhea (≥6 months).

3. Any of the following pap smear results:
o Presence of AGC-endometrial.
o Presence of AGC-all subcategories other than endometrial – If ≥35 years of age or at risk for endometrial
cancer (risk factors or symptoms).
o Presence of benign-appearing endometrial cells in patients ≥40 years of age who also have abnormal
uterine bleeding or risk factors for endometrial cancer.


2) Pap smear for the following indications:
1. Cervical pathology suspected.
2. Screening due.
3. Postcoital bleeding or abnormal cervix on exam.

3) Office hysteroscopy for the following indications:
1. Intracavitary lesion suspected.
2. Persistent bleeding with nondiagnostic imaging.
3. Need for immediate visualization plus biopsy/removal.

Clinical and/or biochemical signs of hyperandrogenism (If labs needed, use the calculated free testosterone,
calculated bioavailable testosterone, or free androgen index “Not DHEAS”)

measuring 2–9 mm in one or both ovaries).

Guideline:

Severe Asthma – Biologic Therapy

Definitions:

1. Asthma: A heterogeneous chronic inflammatory airway disease characterized by variable respiratory symptoms
(wheeze, shortness of breath, chest tightness, cough) and variable expiratory airflow limitation.

2. Difficult-to-Treat Asthma: Persistent asthma symptoms and/or exacerbations despite prescribing of medium or
high-dose inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) combined with another controller (e.g., LABA), or maintenance oral
corticosteroids (OCS), after confirmation of diagnosis, treatment adherence, and comorbidity management.

3. Severe Asthma: Asthma requiring high-dose ICS plus a second controller (e.g., LABA ± LAMA) to prevent it from
becoming uncontrolled, ORasthma that remains uncontrolled despite this therapy. Specifically, BOTH of the following
must be present:
• Demonstrated variable airflow limitation (spirometry or bronchoprovocation testing).
• Frequent or persistent symptoms: cough, wheeze, or dyspnea >2 times/week; activity limitation; nocturnal
awakening; AND/OR frequent exacerbations (≥1 hospitalization or ≥2 OCS-requiring exacerbations per year).

4. Type 2 (T2) Airway Inflammation: The predominant inflammatory endotype in severe asthma, driven by Th2
cytokines (IL-4, IL-5, IL-13) and upstream alarmins (TSLP, IL-33). Characterized by eosinophilic inflammation, elevated
FeNO, and IgE-mediated allergic sensitization.

5. Blood Eosinophil Count (BEC): A key biomarker for T2 inflammation, measured as cells/µL.

6. Fractional Exhaled Nitric Oxide (FeNO): A non-invasive biomarker of eosinophilic airway inflammation,
expressed in parts per billion (ppb).

7. Biologic Therapy (Add-on): Monoclonal antibodies targeting specific molecular pathways involved in T2 airway
inflammation, used as add-on therapy at GINA Step 5 for severe uncontrolled asthma.


Approved biologic classes:
§ Anti-IgE: Omalizumab (Xolair).
§ Anti-IL-5: Mepolizumab.
§ Anti-IL-5 receptor (IL-5Rα): Benralizumab.
§ Anti-IL-4 receptor α (IL-4Rα, targeting IL-4 and IL-13): Dupilumab (Dupixent).
§ Anti-TSLP (thymic stromal lymphopoietin): Tezepelumab.


Scope:
This guideline applies to the coverage evaluation of biologic add-on therapy for patients presenting with:
• Confirmed severe asthma at GINA Step 5 (uncontrolled on high-dose ICS-LABA ± LAMA).
• Adolescents (≥12 years) and adults, except where a specific biologic is approved from age ≥6.
• Referral from a specialist (pulmonologist or allergist/immunologist).

This guideline does NOTcover:
• Mild-to-moderate asthma not meeting Step 5 criteria.
• First-line or step-down controller therapy.
• Acute exacerbation management.
• Non-asthma indications for the same biologics (e.g., atopic dermatitis, nasal polyposis).
• Pediatric patients under age 6.
• Non-biologic management protocols.


Policy:
Requirements for coverage

Documentation requirements:

• Confirmed asthma diagnosis with spirometric evidence of variable airflow limitation.
• GINA Step 5 treatment failure: documented high-dose ICS-LABA (± LAMA) use for ≥3 months with persistent
uncontrolled asthma.
• Evidence of adherence to current therapy and correct inhaler technique.
• Documented assessment and optimization of modifiable risk factors and comorbidities (rhinosinusitis, GERD,
obesity, OSA, anxiety/depression).
• Specialist referral (pulmonologist or allergist/immunologist) with documented phenotyping and biomarker
assessment.
• Documented asthma control level (ACQ-6 or ACT score) and exacerbation history in the prior 12 months.



Coverage criteria - Pre-Biologic Evaluation:

The following workup must be completed and documented prior to biologic initiation:

1) Confirm diagnosis and rule out alternatives:
• Spirometry with bronchodilator reversibility (≥12% and 200 mL increase in FEV1, OR bronchoprovocation if
pre-BD spirometry is normal).
• Rule out vocal cord dysfunction, COPD, bronchiectasis, cardiac causes.

2) Baseline laboratory testing:
• Full blood count with differential (BEC).
• Total serum IgE.
• Skin-prick testing (SPT) ORallergen-specific serum IgE (for allergic phenotyping).
• FeNO measurement (if available).
• Spirometry (FEV1, FVC, FEV1/FVC) — current values and historical.

3) Biomarker thresholds for T2 inflammation (GINA 2025):
• BEC ≥300 cells/µL: typical threshold for T2-targeted biologic eligibility.
• BEC ≥150 cells/µL: suggests T2 inflammation; may meet threshold in clinical context.
• FeNO >50 ppb (ICS-naïve); FeNO ≥25 ppb (medium-dose ICS); FeNO ≥20 ppb (high-dose ICS): elevated
threshold values.
• Note: BEC and FeNO should be measured ≥3 times if not initially above target threshold. Oral corticosteroids
suppress eosinophils and FeNO — historical values preferred when patient is on OCS.

4) Exacerbation burden (minimum required for coverage):
• ≥2 severe exacerbations requiring systemic OCS in the past 12 months, OR
• ≥1 hospitalization for asthma in the past 12 months, OR
• Maintenance OCS dependence (ongoing use ≥3 months to maintain asthma control).

Coverage criteria - Agent-Specific Eligibility:

1) Omalizumab “Xolair” – Anti-IgE:
• Confirmed sensitization to at least one perennial inhaled allergen (positive SPT ≥3mm or allergen-specific IgE
≥0.35 kU/L).
• Total serum IgE 30–1500 IU/mL.
• Body weight and IgE level within the approved dosing table.
• Note: Omalizumab has no well-established OCS-sparing effect — use with caution in maintenance OCS-
dependent patients.


2) Mepolizumab – Anti-IL-5:
• BEC ≥150 cells/µL while on high-dose ICS, OR ≥300 cells/µL at any point in the prior 12 months.
• Preferred agent when nasal polyposis is a comorbidity (also approved for CRSwNP).
• Approved from age ≥6 years.

3) Benralizumab – Anti-IL-5Rα:
• BEC ≥150 cells/µL while on high-dose ICS, OR ≥300 cells/µL at any point in the prior 12 months.
• Often preferred for dosing convenience (every 8 weeks after initial loading doses).
• Approved from age ≥12 years.

4) Dupilumab (Dupixent ) – Anti-IL-4Rα:
• BEC ≥150 cells/µL OR FeNO ≥20–25 ppb (consistent with T2-high profile).
• Preferred in OCS-dependent patients (established OCS-sparing efficacy).
• Preferred when atopic comorbidities coexist (atopic dermatitis, eosinophilic esophagitis — also approved for
these indications).
• Approved from age ≥6 years.

5) Tezepelumab – Anti-TSLP:
• No mandatory BEC or FeNO threshold required for eligibility.
• Approved for severe uncontrolled asthma in patients aged ≥12 years, regardless of eosinophilic phenotype.
• First-line option when BEC <150 cells/µL and no T2 biomarker signal is present (T2-low phenotype).
• Also shows increased efficacy in T2-high patients (elevated BEC or FeNO).

Coverage criteria - Biologic Comorbidity Alignment:

When a relevant T2 comorbidity exists, coverage should preferentially align with a single biologic agent approved for
both asthma and the comorbidity:

Coverage criteria - Treatment Response and Continuation:

All biologic approvals are conditional on demonstrated clinical response. Reassessment must occur at 4–6 months after
initiation. Continuation requires documentation of ≥1 of the following response criteria:
• ≥50% reduction in annualized exacerbation rate.
• ≥50% reduction in maintenance OCS dose (OCS-dependent patients).
• Clinically meaningful improvement in asthma control score (ACQ-6 decrease ≥0.5, or ACT increase ≥3 points).
• Meaningful improvement in FEV1 or quality of life in clinical judgment.

If inadequate response at 4–6 months:
• Reassess diagnosis, adherence, and comorbidities.
• Consider switching to an alternative biologic from a different class if patient meets eligibility criteria.
• Macrolide therapy (low-dose azithromycin) and/or low-dose maintenance OCS are reasonable when no biologic
option is available or effective.


Biologic discontinuation:
• A trial of discontinuation should not be considered until after ≥12 months of treatment with well-maintained
asthma control.
• Only consider if asthma remains well-controlled on at least medium-dose ICS-containing therapy.
• For allergic asthma (omalizumab “Xolair”): ensure no ongoing relevant allergen exposure before discontinuation.

Guideline: Clinical Indications and Frequency of Treatment for Botulinum Toxin Type A Injections
in Chronic Migraine

Definitions:
Chronic migraine: headache occurring on 15 or more days per month for more than three months, with the
features of migraine headache on at least eight of those days.

Episodic migraine: headache occurring on fewer than 15 days per month.

Preventive (prophylactic) medicine: an agent taken regularly to reduce the frequency and severity of
migraine attacks, as distinct from the acute treatment of an individual attack.

Treatment cycle: a single administration of onabotulinumtoxinA across the full set of injection sites; cycles
are given no more often than every 12 weeks.

Scope:
This guideline covers requests for botulinum toxin type A (onabotulinumtoxinA) given by intramuscular
injection for the prevention of chronic migraine in adults, for both the initial course of treatment and for
continuation beyond that course.

This guideline does NOT cover:
• Episodic migraine, that is fewer than 15 headache days per month.
• Tension-type headache, cluster headache, trigeminal neuralgia, cervicogenic headache and all other
headache disorders.
• The acute treatment of a migraine attack.
• Patients under 18 years of age.
• Botulinum toxin preparations other than onabotulinumtoxinA. Botulinum toxin products are not
interchangeable and their potency units cannot be converted between preparations.

Policy:
Botulinum toxin type A is covered for the prevention of chronic migraine only where all of criteria A,
B and C are met.


A: The patient is aged 18 years or over and has a diagnosis of chronic migraine made by a neurologist, that is
headache on 15 or more days per month for more than three months with migraine features on at least eight
of those days, recorded on a headache diary.

B: At least three preventive medicines have not worked, were not tolerated, or are unsuitable on safety
grounds. Each oral agent must have been taken for at least eight weeks at the target dose before being judged
to have failed.

C: Where acute headache medication is overused, the overuse has been identified and the medication
withdrawn before treatment begins.

Covered dose and frequency:
The covered regimen is onabotulinumtoxinA 155 units, given as 5 units per 0.1 mL at each of 31 injection
sites divided bilaterally as set out in Table 1, repeated once every 12 weeks. An initial course of three cycles
is covered.

Doses above 155 units, injections at more than 31 sites, and repeat injection earlier than 12 weeks after the
previous cycle are not covered.

Continuation of treatment:
A fourth or subsequent cycle is covered only where all of the following are met.

• Three cycles have been completed, each given at least 12 weeks apart, with a headache diary kept
throughout.
• Headache days per month have fallen by at least 30 per cent compared with the headache diary kept
before the first cycle.
• The condition has not changed to episodic migraine, that is fewer than 15 headache days per month, for
three consecutive months.
Where these are met, one further cycle is covered, to be given no earlier than 12 weeks after the previous
cycle. Treatment is not covered once the condition has been episodic migraine for three consecutive months.

Documentation Requirements:
1. A neurologist report stating the diagnosis of chronic migraine and the date it was made.
2. The headache diary covering the month before the request, showing headache days and migraine days.
3. The names, doses and durations of the preventive medicines tried, with the reason each was stopped.
4. For a continuation request, the dates of the previous cycles, the units given at each, and the headache
diary kept before the first cycle.
5. ICD-10 and SBS codes coded to the highest level of specificity and accuracy.

Guideline: Chronic Diseases Management (CDM) – Dyslipidemia

Dyslipidemia

Screening for normal Asymptomatic population:

Guideline:


Definition:

Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) refers to the complex of symptoms and signs brought on by compression of the median nerve as it
travels through the carpal tunnel. Patients commonly experience pain and paresthesia, and less commonly weakness, in the
median nerve distribution.

CTS categorized based on clinical symptoms into:
- Mild symptoms: non-persistent numbness or weakness. Symptoms do not disrupt sleep, impair hand function, or interfere with
activities of daily living (ADLs).
- Moderate symptoms: Persistent numbness or mild nocturnal symptoms occasionally disrupt sleep. Symptoms may interfere slightly
with hand function, but the patient is able to perform all ADLs.
- Severe CTS symptoms: Symptoms are disabling, routinely disrupt sleep, or prevent the patient from carrying out one or more ADLs.

CTS further categorized based on electrodiagnostic testing into:
- Mild CTS: prolonged (relative or absolute) sensory latencies; motor studies are normal. There is no evidence for axon loss.
- Moderate: prolonged sensory and motor latencies. There is no evidence of axon loss.
- Severe: characterized by evidence of axon loss, as defined by any of the following:
o Absent or low-amplitude sensory nerve action potential (SNAP) or mixed nerve action potential
o Low-amplitude or absent thenar compound muscle action potential (CMAP)
o Needle electromyography (EMG) with fibrillation potentials or motor unit potential changes



Scope:

This guideline outlined the diagnosis, management of carpal tunnel syndrome


Policy:
• Eligibility/coverage criteria:
o Diagnosis:
- Carpal Tunnel Syndrome (CTS) is primarily a clinical diagnosis based on characteristic symptoms and physical findings.

- Diagnostic testing is indicated in patients with moderate to severe symptoms or when the diagnosis is uncertain. It may also be

considered in patients with mild symptoms who show disease progression despite optimal conservative management.

- Nerve Conduction Study (NCS): Initial electrodiagnostic test and is recommended for patients with moderate to severe or atypical

symptoms.

- Electromyography (EMG): Reserved for patients with atypical symptoms to exclude alternative diagnoses or when nerve

decompression surgery is being considered.

- Imaging (Ultrasound or MRI): Performed only in patients with atypical presentations where electrodiagnostic studies fail to explain

the symptoms. It is useful for identifying anatomical variants or secondary causes of CTS, such as tumors, ganglion cyst, bifid median

nerve, or bone abnormalities.

o Management:
- First-line:
Wrist splinting ± corticosteroid injection — Recommended for all patients, including those with moderate to severe symptoms,
provided there is no evidence of axonal loss.
- Second-line:
Physical therapy (Modalities: Carpal bones Mobilization/Manual therapy, Nerve gliding exercises, or therapeutic ultrasound) Offered
to patients who do not respond to 1st line therapy provided there is no axonal loss or worsening of symptoms.
- Third-line:
Nerve decompression surgery — Indicated for patients with evidence of axonal loss, progressive neurological symptoms, or failure of
conservative (non-surgical) management.

• Requirements for Coverage
o ICD-10 and SBS codes must be coded to the highest level of specificity


• Insurance Documentation Requirement:
o Initial diagnosis report
- Comprehensive details on symptoms, signs, diagnostic testing, and severity level
o Treatment records
- Documented prescribed treatment, duration and patient response


• Non-coverage:
o The following treatment has no evidence and shall not be covered:
- NSAIDs
- Electrical, magnetic, and laser therapy
- Perineural dextrose injections

Guideline: Diagnostic approach for celiac disease and frequency of follow up investigations


Definition:

Celiac disease is a chronic immune-mediated systemic disorder triggered by dietary gluten in genetically predisposed
individuals, resulting in inflammation and villous atrophy of the small intestine. Clinical manifestations range from classic
gastrointestinal symptoms to extraintestinal manifestations such as iron deficiency anemia, osteoporosis, elevated liver
enzymes, infertility, and neurologic symptoms. Accurate diagnosis is essential because treatment requires lifelong
adherence to a gluten-free diet, while unnecessary dietary restriction should be avoided in patients without confirmed
disease. This guideline outlines the evidence-based diagnostic approach and medically necessary follow-up
investigations to support appropriate clinical care and insurance coverage.

Scope:

This guideline applies to:
• Adults and children with suspected celiac disease.
• Individuals belonging to recognized high-risk groups requiring screening.
• Patients with confirmed celiac disease requiring follow-up monitoring.

Intended users are family physicians, gastroenterologists, pediatricians, internal medicine physicians, insurance
medical reviewers and medical directors. Healthcare settings include primary care, specialty outpatient clinics,
hospital outpatient departments and health insurance medical review

Policy:
• Requirements for coverage

1. Initial diagnostic evaluation

Coverage is recommended when one of the following are present:
Clinical features suggestive of celiac disease, or being in an established high-risk group.

• IgG-based serologic testing (e.g., DGP-IgG or tTG-IgG)

Endoscopic biopsy

• Discordance between clinical findings and serology.


Routine repeat biopsy is not covered following successful treatment unless clinically indicated.

3. Baseline assessment after confirmed diagnosis
Coverage is recommended for:
• Complete blood count (CBC)
• Ferritin (iron stores)
• Vitamin D
• Liver function tests (if clinically indicated)
• Comprehensive dietary assessment by a dietitian experienced in gluten-free diets
Additional nutritional investigations should be reserved for patients with evidence of malnutrition or severe
malabsorption.

Guideline: Common Clinical Indications for Cervical MRI

Definition:

Neck pain, for the purposes of this guideline, is classified as:

• Acute/traumatic cervical pain: onset following a defined traumatic event (motor vehicle collision, fall, direct blow, sports
injury, diving injury).
• Chronic/non-traumatic (atraumatic) cervical pain: persistent or recurrent neck pain, with or without radiculopathy, present
for more than 6 weeks without a clear inciting traumatic event, including degenerative, inflammatory, and mechanical etiologies.
• Cervical radiculopathy: neck pain radiating into the shoulder, arm, or hand, with or without associated sensory, motor, or reflex
changes, attributable to nerve root involvement.

Scope:
This guideline applies to all requests for cervical spine MRI submitted for prior authorization or claims adjudication for Insured
members presenting with neck pain, with or without radiculopathy or myelopathic features, whether traumatic or non-traumatic
in origin, across outpatient, emergency, and inpatient settings.


This guideline does NOT cover:
- Occupational injury: Injury arising directly from the profession of the Insured.
- Personal risk activities: injury due to personal risk activities such as dangerous sports (judo, boxing, karate, wrestling, combat
sports), motor/boat/motorcycle racing, paragliding, parachuting.
- Insufficient documentation: no clear duration, mechanism, exam findings, or suspected diagnosis
- Acute traumatic neck injury (as initial imaging): use cervical CT as initial.
o MRI may be indicated when CT is normal; however, upper-extremity paresthesia or focal neurological deficits, such as
weakness, suggest spinal cord injury.

Policy:

Requirements for coverage
- Documentation must include duration, mechanism (traumatic vs non-traumatic), severity, examination findings, Prior imaging if
present and evidence of conservative management and its outcome, where applicable to the clinical scenario.
- ICD-10 and SBS codes must be submitted at the highest level of specificity.


1) Acute / Traumatic Neck Pain:

1.1 Cervical MRI is indicated if (after the initial cervical CT):

• Upper extremity paresthesias or focal neurologic findings (eg, extremity weakness, gait or coordination difficulty, bladder
or bowel dysfunction, or Lhermitte sign), even when the CT is normal.
• Suspected or confirmed ligamentous, spinal cord or nerve root injury, with or without trauma identified on CT.

2) Red-Flag / Urgent Indications:

2.1 The following presentations warrant expedited MRI approval:
- Fever, chills, and/or night sweats
- Unexplained weight loss
- Immunosuppression (eg, concurrent chemotherapy or immunosuppressive therapy)
- Active or prior malignancy
- History of inflammatory arthritis
- Intravenous recreational drug use
- Active anticoagulant therapy
- Age ≥60 years

2.2 Cervical spondylotic myelopathy (compressive cervical cord myelopathy):
- Progressive limb weakness.
- Numbness, gait or coordination difficulty.
- Hyperreflexia/clonus.
- Bowel or bladder dysfunction.
- Lhermitte sign (forward flexion of the neck elicits an electric shock-like sensation in the neck, radiating down the spine or
into the arms.)

3) Chronic/ cervical radiculopathy without red flags:

3.1 MRI is indicated if:
- Symptoms persist despite 6–8 weeks of appropriate conservative treatment
o Documentation is required of the treatment provided
o Failure of conservative treatment is defined as:
§ persistent moderate-to-severe pain with inadequate improvement and continued interference with sleep, daily
activities, or work.

Guideline: Admission & Discharge Criteria for DKA/HHS


Definition:

Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA): Defined by the biochemical triad of ketonemia, hyperglycemia and acidemia.

Diagnostic Criteria for DKA: (All 3 biochemical criteria are required for the diagnosis)
• Plasma glucose (PG) more than or equal to 200 mg/dl (11.1 mmol/L) or known diabetes;
• Positive serum ketones or significant ketonuria (more than or equal to 2+ urine ketone) and;
• Venous or arterial HCO3 less than 15 mmol/L and/ or pH less than 7.3.

Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS): is a syndrome characterized by severe hyperglycemia, hyperosmolality, and
dehydration in the absence of ketoacidosis.

Diagnostic Criteria of HHS :
• Marked Hyperglycemia: plasma glucose > 540 mg/dL (30 mmol/L), without significant hyperketonemia ( negative urine
ketones or trace) or acidosis ( PH > 7.3, serum Bicarbonate > 15).
Plus
• Serum Osmolality > 320 mOsmol/kg. “Formula for calculating serum Osmolality={ 2X (Na) + Glucose(mmol/L) + Urea
(mmol/L)”


Scope:

This guideline applies to insurance coverage decisions for:
- Hospital admission for suspected or confirmed DKA/HHS
- Safe discharge criteria

This guideline does NOT cover:
- Hyperglycemia not meeting DKA/HHS diagnostic criteria
- Admission requests with insufficient documentation, such as no clear symptoms, vital signs, mental status, laboratory criteria,
treatment course, or response to treatment


Policy:
• Requirements for coverage
- Documentation must include the presenting symptoms, vital signs, mental status, relevant laboratory results, treatment
provided, response to treatment, and discharge readiness when applicable.
- ICD-10 and SBS codes must be submitted at the highest level of specificity.

1. DKA/HHS Admission Criteria:

Markers of severity (Manage in HDU/ICU): Any 1 severity marker is enough to consider HDU/ICU care.
• GCS less than 12
• pH less than 7.1
• Serum ketones more than 6 mmol/L
• HCO3 less than 5 mmol/L ( some resources <10mmol/L)
• K⁺ less than 3.3 or more than 6.0 mmol/L
• SBP less than 90 mmHg
• SpO2 less than 92% in room air and pulse rate more than 100 or less than 60 bpm
• Urine output less than 0.5 ml/kg/hr or evidence of acute kidney injury


2. Discharge Criteria

2.1 DKA Resolution criteria:
- Blood or serum beta-hydroxybutyrate <0.6 mmol/L or normalization of the serum anion gap (≤12 mEq/L).
- Venous pH ≥7.3 or serum bicarbonate ≥18 mmol/L – In patients who received isotonic saline, monitoring for resolution of
acidosis may be complicated by the evolution a hyperchloremic, non-anion gap acidosis. Hyperchloremic acidosis does
not indicate unresolved DKA. (See 'Hyperchloremic acidosis' below.)
- Serum glucose <200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L).

2.2 HHS Resolution criteria
- Calculated effective Posm is <300 mOsmol/kg
- Serum glucose is <250 mg/dL (13.9 mmol/L)
- Urine output is >0.5 mL/kg per hour
- Cognitive status has returned to baseline

pages:
Title: Diabetes Screening


Overview:
Diabetes mellitus (DM) is a chronic metabolic disorder characterized by elevated blood glucose levels resulting, persistent
hyperglycemia is associated with long-term damage to various organs, especially the eyes, kidneys, nerves, heart, and
blood vessels. Because diabetes often remains asymptomatic in its early stages, many individuals are unaware of their
condition until complications develop. Screening for diabetes helps in early identification, timely intervention, and
prevention of long-term complications.
Screening can be done via various laboratory tests methods such as Hemoglobin A1C (HgA1C), Fasting blood sugar (FBS),
75 oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT), each has its own advantages and disadvantages.


Scope:
• These guidelines cover the screening for General Healthy Population.
• This guideline does not cover Individuals high-risk groups (e.g. On immunosuppressant therapy, Cystic fibrosis patients,
post-transplant, …)
Policy:
• Eligibility/coverage criteria:



o Screening using one test (FBS, A1C, OGTT)
▪ Above 35 years of age
• No screening done in the past 3 years, or in the past 1 year if risk factor presents (Table 2)
▪ 18 – 35 years of age
• Overweight or Obesity (BMI ≥25 kg/m2) and at least one of the risk factors (Table 2)
▪ 10 – 18 years of age
• Overweight (≥85th percentile) or Obesity (≥95th percentile) and
1. T2DM in a first-degree relative
2. Signs or conditions associated with insulin resistance (e.g., hypertension, dyslipidemia,
acanthosis nigricans, polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), or small for gestational age birth
weight).
3. Maternal history of DM or GDM during the child's gestation
▪ People with prediabetes (Table 1)
• To be screened once a year.
▪ Pregnant 15 weeks before gestation
• Only if risk factor present (Table 2)
o Screening for Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM)
▪ Screening for GDM is done once at 24 – 28 Weeks using 75-g OGTT
o Routine screening for T1DM is not recommended.

Criteria defining prediabetes in nonpregnant individuals


A1C 5.7–6.4% (39–47 mmol/mol)

OR


FPG 100 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L) to 125 mg/dL (6.9 mmol/L)

OR


2-h PG during 75-g OGTT 140 mg/dL (7.8 mmol/L) to 199 mg/dL (11.0 mmol/L)



Risk factors associated with T2DM
• First-degree relative with diabetes (Father, Mother, Brother, Sister)

• History of cardiovascular disease
• Hypertension (≥140/80 mmHg or on therapy for hypertension)
• HDL cholesterol level <35 mg/dL (<0.9 mmol/L) and/or triglyceride level >250 mg/dL (>2.8 mmol/L)
• Ladies with history of GDM
• Individuals with polycystic ovary syndrome

• Physical inactivity

• Other clinical conditions associated with insulin resistance (e.g., acanthosis nigricans, metabolic
dysfunction–associated Steatosis liver disease)
• HIV infection
• Individuals Obstructive sleep apnea
• Individuals with Cystic fibrosis
• Use of drugs associated with diabetes: glucocorticoids, atypical antipsychotics, statins, highly active
antiretroviral therapy, anti-rejection drugs, thiazide diuretics.

pages:
Guideline:

Dyslipidemia – Advanced Lipid-Lowering Therapy: Biologic & Novel Agent
Definitions:

1) Dyslipidemia: Abnormal levels of one or more lipid fractions: elevated LDL-C, non-HDL-C, triglycerides (TG), or
Lp(a); or reduced HDL-C. Causally associated with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD).
2) ASCVD (Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease): Includes coronary artery disease (CAD/MI), ischemic
stroke/TIA, symptomatic peripheral artery disease (PAD), and other atherosclerotic vascular events.
3) ApoB (Apolipoprotein B): One particle per atherogenic lipoprotein; more strongly associated with ASCVD events
than LDL-C when using Friedewald estimation. Useful when LDL-C and apoB are discordant. Target: <65 mg/dL
(very high risk), <80 mg/dL (high risk).
4) Lp(a) (Lipoprotein(a)): A genetically determined, causal, independent ASCVD risk factor not captured by
standard lipid panels. Universal once-in-a-lifetime screening is a Class I (Level A) recommendation in 2026
ACC/AHA. Threshold of clinical significance: ≥125 nmol/L (≥50 mg/dL).
5) Familial Hypercholesterolemia (FH):
• Heterozygous FH (HeFH): Autosomal dominant mutation causing LDL-C typically 160–400 mg/dL. Prevalence
~1:250. Diagnosed by Dutch Lipid Clinic Network (DLCN) or Simon Broome criteria, or genetic testing.
• Homozygous FH (HoFH): Biallelic mutations; LDL-C often >400 mg/dL; extremely high ASCVD risk; requires
specialized therapies including PCSK9i, evinacumab, and/or lomitapide.
6) PCSK9 Inhibitors (Biologics):
• Monoclonal antibodies (evolocumab “Repatha”, alirocumab “Praluent”) targeting PCSK9 — a serine protease
that degrades LDL receptors. Inhibition upregulates hepatic LDL-R, reducing LDL-C by 50–65% on top of statin
therapy.
• Inclisiran “Leqvio”: A small interfering RNA (siRNA) — not a monoclonal antibody but a biologic-class agent
— that silences PCSK9 synthesis in hepatocytes. Twice-yearly SC dosing. Similar LDL-C reduction to mAbs.
7) Evinacumab: The only agent effective in HoFH with absent LDL-R activity.
8) Maximally Tolerated Statin Therapy (MTST): The highest statin dose the patient can tolerate without
unacceptable muscle or other adverse effects, including high-intensity statin (rosuvastatin 20–40 mg or atorvastatin
40–80 mg) or moderate-intensity if intolerant. MTST is a prerequisite before most advanced agents.





1

Scope:

This guideline applies to the coverage evaluation of advanced lipid-lowering therapy (PCSK9 inhibitors, inclisiran,
evinacumab, bempedoic acid, and other novel agents) for:
• Adults with clinical ASCVD (secondary prevention) not at LDL-C goal on MTST ± ezetimibe.
• Adults with familial hypercholesterolemia (HeFH or HoFH) not at goal on MTST ± ezetimibe.
• Adults with severe hypercholesterolemia (LDL-C ≥190 mg/dL) without FH criteria, not at goal.
• Adults with high-risk primary prevention profiles (diabetes, CKD, Lp(a) ≥125 nmol/L) not at goal.
• Adults with confirmed statin intolerance requiring alternative non-statin agents.

This guideline does NOTcover:
• Mild or moderate dyslipidemia manageable with lifestyle + standard statin therapy.
• Management of isolated hypertriglyceridemia without elevated ASCVD risk.
• Dyslipidemia management in children <10 years.





Policy:

Requirements for coverage

Documentation requirements:

• Fasting lipid panel (LDL-C, non-HDL-C, HDL-C, TG, TC) within the past 3 months — minimum 2 values on
different occasions to confirm persistent elevation.
• Evidence of MTST ± ezetimibe for ≥3 months (or documented statin intolerance with ≥2 statin trials at different
doses with symptom resolution after discontinuation).
• ASCVD risk category documentation: clinical ASCVD diagnosis, FH diagnosis, or 10-year ASCVD risk estimate
using PREVENT-ASCVD equations (per 2026 ACC/AHA) or PCE.
• Specialist referral letter (cardiologist, lipidologist, or internal medicine specialist) confirming: risk category,
therapy failure, proposed agent, and LDL-C target.
• Documented lifestyle optimization: heart-healthy diet and physical activity counseling within the past 12 months.
• Documented Lp(a) measurement at least once (Class I, 2026 ACC/AHA) — results must be available at time of
advanced therapy request.





Coverage criteria - Pre-Treatment Investigations (Tiered Approach):
To avoid unnecessary cost burden while ensuring clinically appropriate agent selection, investigations are stratified into
three coverage tiers:





2

TIER 1 — Mandatory for ALL advanced lipid therapy coverage requests

Requiredateverycoveragerequest,regardlessofagentrequested:
• Fasting lipid panel: LDL-C (Martin/Hopkins preferred), non-HDL-C, HDL-C, TG, TC — ≥2 measurements
on separate occasions at least 4 weeks apart.
• Liver function tests (ALT/AST): baseline prior to initiation; required for ezetimibe, bempedoic acid, and
statin documentation.
• Creatinine / eGFR: renal function affects risk category classification (CKD stage 3 = high risk, stage 4–5
= very high risk per Saudi 2022 guidelines).
• Documentation of statin therapy history: agent, dose, duration, and tolerability. Minimum: MTST for
≥3 months, OR ≥2 documented statin trials with intolerance with symptom resolution after discontinuation.
• PREVENT-ASCVD 10-year risk estimate (or equivalent: PCE, SCORE2) — for primary prevention patients
only. Not required for known ASCVD or confirmed FH.
• Lp(a) measurement: at least once per lifetime (Class I, 2026 ACC/AHA). Should be documented before
approval of any advanced agent in primary prevention. If already measured and documented, repeat is not
required.


TIER 2 — Conditional: Required only when the candidate agent or clinical indication demands it

Not required for every request — ordered only when the specific agent or phenotype being requested requires the result:
A) ApoB (Apolipoprotein B):
• Required when: LDL-C appears at goal but clinical suspicion of residual atherogenic risk persists (e.g.,
hypertriglyceridemia with elevated TG-rich remnants, metabolic syndrome, diabetes). ApoB can support decisions to
intensify therapy even when LDL-C appears controlled (2026 ACC/AHA).
• NOT required when: LDL-C is clearly above goal and agent selection does not depend on apoB.
B) Genetic Testing for FH (LDLR, APOB, PCSK9 mutations):
• Required when: Requesting evinacumab for HoFH (genetic confirmation of biallelic FH mutations required by
indication).
• Required when: Clinical FH diagnosis is uncertain (borderline DLCN score 3–5) and genetic confirmation would
change agent eligibility.
• NOT required when: Clinical FH diagnosis is definite (DLCN score ≥6, or Simon Broome definite) — clinical diagnosis
is sufficient for PCSK9 inhibitor approval.
C) hsCRP (High-sensitivity C-reactive protein):
• Conditional use as a risk-reclassification tool in intermediate-risk primary prevention patients where treatment
decision is borderline. Per 2026 ACC/AHA: hsCRP ≥2.0 mg/L supports reclassification to higher risk and earlier
statin/PCSK9i initiation.
• NOT required as standard workup for all secondary prevention or FH patients.
D) Coronary Artery Calcium (CAC) Score:
• Conditional for primary prevention: CAC =0 supports deferring pharmacotherapy in borderline-risk patients; CAC
≥100 AU or ≥75th percentile supports LDL-C goal <70 mg/dL; CAC ≥1000 AU supports goal <55 mg/dL (2026
ACC/AHA).
• NOT required for known ASCVD, FH, or diabetes patients — risk category is already established.




3

TIER 3 — Specialist-Discretion: Not required for routine coverage approval

• Lipoprotein fractionation / NMR particle testing: may assist in lipid phenotyping but not required for agent
eligibility determination.
• PCSK9 serum levels: research use only; not a coverage prerequisite.
• Fatty liver imaging (FibroScan, MRI-PDFF): relevant for NAFLD/MASLD context but not required for lipid
agent approval.
• Cardiac imaging (echocardiogram, stress testing): cardiovascular workup may support risk stratification but
is not a prerequisite for lipid therapy approval.

Guideline: Ganglion Cyst


Overview:
Ganglion cysts are benign, fluid-filled masses arising from joints or tendon sheaths, most commonly in the wrist
and hand. They often fluctuate in size and may resolve spontaneously. Management is symptom-driven, focusing
on functional limitation, pain, neurovascular compromise, or persistent patient discomfort. Evidence-based
practice supports conservative management as first line, with surgical referral reserved for cases with recurrent
symptoms, mechanical interference, or confirmed structural impact. This guideline standardizes evaluation and
intervention thresholds to ensure clinically appropriate, cost-aligned, and consistent decision-making.

Scope:
▪ This guideline covers the general diagnosis and treatment of ganglion cyst.

Policy:

• Diagnosis:
o Most ganglion cysts are clinical diagnosis with physical examination.
o Imaging: While radiographs are generally not helpful, an ultrasound or MRI can be useful for assessing
the cyst's size, location, and relationship to surrounding structures, particularly in complex cases.


• Management:
o Management is based on symptoms:
▪ Asymptomatic ganglion cyst: Requires no intervention.
▪ Mild to Moderate symptoms: Conservative therapy (Analgesia, Compression/Brace).
▪ Severe: Surgical Treatment.


The conditions described below would be regarded as severe in this respect:
• Ganglion on wrist with evidence of neurovascular compromise or significant pain.
• Seed ganglia at base of digits with significant pain.
• Mucoid cysts at the distal interphalangeal joint which has disrupted the nail growth or
there are cysts that tend to discharge.
• Ganglia on foot and ankles with evidence of neurovascular compromise or significant pain
or causing difficulties with footwear or mobility.
• Restriction of activities of daily living.
• Persistent or recurrent symptoms despite initial treatment with conservative
therapy.
▪ Injection of ganglion cyst with glucocorticoids is not recommended.
▪ Aspiration is not routinely recommended due to high recurrence rate.
▪ Physiotherapy has no role in the treatment of ganglion cyst itself.
o Post-surgery Stiffness and decrease range of motion may occur which may require physiotherapy
sessions (Up to 18 sessions)

Title: Hemorrhoids


Overview:
Hemorrhoids are common anorectal condition that cause bleeding, and discomfort, often related to
constipation or straining. Most cases can be effectively managed in primary care through lifestyle modification

Guideline: Clinical Indications and Dispensing Criteria for Human Immunoglobulin (IVIG / SCIG)
in Chronic Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyradiculoneuropathy (CIDP)


Definitions:
Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (CIDP): an acquired, immune-mediated
neuropathy characterised by chronicity, demyelination and inflammation. In the classic form motor
involvement exceeds sensory. The course is slowly progressive in most patients, with a relapsing–remitting
course in at least one-third. CIDP generally responds to immunomodulatory treatment with glucocorticoids,
IVIG or plasma exchange.


Human Immunoglobulin (IVIG) and subcutaneous immunoglobulin (SCIG): pooled human
immunoglobulin used as an established first-line, disease-modifying therapy for CIDP; improvement is
usually detectable at two to six weeks.


Induction and maintenance treatment: induction is the initial treatment course given to achieve clinical
improvement; maintenance is the ongoing therapy most patients require to sustain that improvement,
individualised over time to the lowest effective dose and longest interval.


Objective treatment response: improvement on at least one disability scale and at least one impairment scale
— for example the Inflammatory Neuropathy Cause and Treatment (INCAT) disability scale, the
Inflammatory Rasch-built Overall Disability Scale (I-RODS), or the Medical Research Council (MRC) sum
score.



Scope:
This guideline governs the medical necessity and pre-authorization of Human Immunoglobulin (IVIG / SCIG)
for children and adults with a confirmed diagnosis of chronic inflammatory demyelinating
polyradiculoneuropathy, in line with the CHI.

This guideline does NOT cover:

• IVIG for benign CIDP that manifests with only distal paraesthesiae and no significant functional
impact — such patients may be monitored without immunomodulatory treatment.
• IVIG for anti-MAG antibody–positive neuropathy (including anti-MAG positive DADS), which is
considered distinct from CIDP, responds suboptimally to IVIG

Policy:
Eligibility and Coverage Criteria:
IVIG is covered as a first-line treatment (Level A) for a patient with a confirmed diagnosis of CIDP when
both A and B are met::

• A: Confirmed diagnosis of CIDP by a neurologist per EAN/PNS criteria, supported by nerve conduction
studies demonstrating demyelination (and, where indicated, supportive CSF, imaging or biopsy findings).

AND

• B: The neuropathy has a significant functional impact (not benign distal paraesthesiae alone).

Prescriber (MD) Requirement:
IVIG must be prescribed by a neurologist.

Re-treatment:
• Maintenance IVIG is covered where an objective response to induction has been documented;
continuation without documented objective benefit at periodic review is not covered.
• If there is no objective response after adequate induction (including the repeated 1 g/kg doses or a second
2 g/kg course), IVIG is considered ineffective and switching to an alternative first-line agent
(corticosteroids or plasma exchange, under their own policies) is appropriate.


Approved Dosing:
• Induction (adults): 2 g/kg total over 2–5 consecutive days (e.g. 0.4 g/kg/day × 5 days); maximum 1
g/kg/day.
• Inadequate first response: give 2–5 further doses of 1 g/kg every 3 weeks, or a second 2 g/kg course,
before judging IVIG ineffective.
• Maintenance (adults): start 1 g/kg every 3 weeks, then individualise to the lowest effective dose / longest
interval (0.4–1 g/kg every 2–6 weeks); assess response after 2–3 months.
• Review and taper: when stable, reduce ~25% per infusion, lengthen the interval, or discontinue —
reviewed every 6–12 months for the first 2–3 years. If end-of-dose deterioration occurs, increase the dose
or shorten the interval.
• Paediatric: no fixed dose — individualise to the lowest effective dose and taper gradually.
• Weight: use adjusted body weight in obesity; avoid the 1 g/kg × 1–2 day regimen where fluid overload
is a concern.


Selection of Agent:
IVIG, corticosteroids, and plasma exchange are all first-line treatments for CIDP (Grade A). The guideline
gives no overall preference between IVIG and corticosteroids, weakly prefers IVIG over plasma exchange.
For maintenance, subcutaneous immunoglobulin (SCIG) is strongly recommended and is a covered alternative
to maintenance IVIG (weakly recommended against for induction); when switching from IVIG to SCIG, start
at the same mean weekly dose (1:1) and tailor to response.

Documentation Requirements:
1. Neurologist note confirming the diagnosis of CIDP (typical or specified variant), the duration of
symptoms (at least eight weeks), and the supporting demyelinating electrodiagnostic findings (± CSF,
imaging or nerve biopsy where performed).
2. Documentation of significant functional impact and the baseline disability / impairment scores (INCAT,
I-RODS or MRC sum score) that will be used to judge treatment response; for maintenance requests, the
objective response to prior IVIG.
3. Anti-MAG antibody status where an atypical distal (DADS) phenotype is present, to exclude anti-MAG
neuropathy.
4. Current weight (kg) — adjusted body weight where obese — for dose calculation, and baseline renal
function (serum creatinine / eGFR).
5. ICD-10 (G61.81) and SBS codes coded to the highest level of specificity and accuracy.

Guideline: Clinical Indications and Dispensing Criteria for Human Immunoglobulin G / Normal
Human Immunoglobulin (IVIG) in Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS)


Definitions:
Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS): an acute, monophasic, immune-mediated paralysing polyneuropathy,
usually preceded by an infection. Immunotherapy with either IVIG or plasma exchange shortens the time to
recovery by approximately 40–50%.

Treatment-related fluctuation (TRF): initial improvement after IVIG or plasma exchange followed by
secondary deterioration; occurs in about 9–10% of patients, typically within 10–60 days of starting treatment.

Intravenous immune globulin (IVIG): pooled human immunoglobulin; the preferred immunomodulatory
agent in most centres for GBS, being better tolerated and easier/quicker to administer than plasma exchange,
with similar efficacy.

GBS disability score (GBS-DS): the functional grade used throughout this guideline to determine coverage.

- Grade 1 — very mildly affected (minor symptoms, still able to run).

- Grade 2 — mild: able to walk unaided but unable to run.

- Grade 3 or more — severe / non-ambulant: unable to walk unaided up to bedbound.

Scope:
This guideline governs the medical necessity and pre-authorization of Human Immunoglobulin G / Normal
Human Immunoglobulin (IVIG) for children, adolescents and adults with a confirmed diagnosis of Guillain-
Barré syndrome, in line with the CHI Formulary Indication Review and the underlying North American and
European clinical guidelines.

This guideline does NOT cover:

• Corticosteroids, which are not recommended in the treatment of GBS (oral corticosteroids are strongly
recommended against; IV methylprednisolone alone or combined with IVIG is weakly recommended
against).
• Sequential / combined treatment with plasma exchange followed immediately by IVIG, which does
not provide a greater effect than either treatment alone and is not covered.
• Milder patients, (a) very mildly affected (grade 1) patients with stable disease; and (b) mild patient
(grade 2) with stable disease presenting >2 weeks after onset.
• Switching to the alternative immune therapy (PE or IVIG) in patients who have not improved or who
deteriorate after the first treatment, as there is no evidence of efficacy for this practice.

Policy:
Eligibility and Coverage Criteria:
IVIG is covered as a first-line therapy for a patient with a confirmed diagnosis of GBS who meets any one of
the three scenarios below. Each scenario has its own treatment window (time from symptom onset); the
prescriber and documentation requirements that follow also apply:

• Scenario 1 — Severe (non-ambulant) GBS. The patient is non-ambulant (GBS-DS grade 3 or more).
Window: start within 4 weeks of onset.
• Scenario 2 — Still-ambulant with a poor-prognostic feature. The patient can still walk but has any
of:
o Fast rate of deterioration.
o Respiratory involvemnt.
o Bulbar involvemnt (swallowing difficulties).
o Autonomic disturbances.
o High mEGOS (≥ 6).
Window: start within 4 weeks of onset.
• Scenario 3 — Still-ambulant, mild and stable (GBS-DS grade 2). The patient has mild, stable or only
slowly deteriorating disease. IVIG is covered on this basis, particularly when other GBS features are
present (arm weakness or cranial-nerve involvement).

Window: start within 2 weeks of onset only.

Presentation more than 4 weeks from onset while still deteriorating falls outside these windows and should
prompt reassessment for acute-onset CIDP or an alternative diagnosis (see algorithm, Appendix 1).


Re-treatment:
• A routine second course of IVIG immediately following the first is not covered, as it does not improve
outcomes and increases adverse effects.
• For a treatment-related fluctuation occurring within the first eight weeks after onset, retreatment with
the same modality initially given is covered.
• In patients who do not clearly improve, or who deteriorate after IVIG or plasma exchange, switching to
the alternative immune therapy is not covered (no evidence of efficacy).
• If progression continues beyond eight weeks, or there are three or more treatment-related fluctuations,
acute-onset CIDP is likely and the diagnosis and treatment pathway should be reviewed.

Prescriber (MD) Requirement:
For adults, IVIG must be prescribed by a consultant neurologist. For paediatric patients, IVIG must be
prescribed by a paediatric neurologist or general paediatrician.

Approved Dosing:
The covered dose of IVIG is 400 mg/kg/dose (0.4 g/kg/day) once daily for five days for both children and
adults (total 2 g/kg). In children, an alternative regimen of 1,000 mg/kg/dose (1 g/kg/day) once daily for two
days is covered. Adjusted body weight is used for weight-based dose calculation in class 1–3 obesity (BMI ≥
30 kg/m²).

It is strongly recommended that patients with a poor prognosis receive only one standard course of
IVIG (0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days); a routinely given second five-day course is not covered.

Selection of Agent:
When both therapies are equally available and there are no contraindications, IVIG is the preferred agent
because it is generally better tolerated and easier to administer than plasma exchange.

Documentation Requirements:
1. Prescriber note — by a consultant neurologist (adults) or paediatric neurologist / general paediatrician
confirming GBS, the date of symptom onset, and functional/disability status.
2. Documentation that the patient is non-ambulant, or ambulant with a poor-prognostic feature (rapid
progression, respiratory/ventilatory risk, swallowing difficulty, or autonomic disturbance).
3. Current weight (kg) — adjusted body weight where BMI ≥ 30 kg/m² — for dose calculation, and baseline
renal function (serum creatinine / eGFR).
4. ICD-10 (G61.0) and SBS codes coded to the highest level of specificity and accuracy.

documents.title: Myasthenia Gravis – IVIG
pages:
Guideline: Clinical Indications and Dispensing Criteria for Human Immunoglobulin G / Normal
Human Immunoglobulin (IVIG) in Myasthenia Gravis


Definitions:
Myasthenia gravis (MG): an autoimmune disorder of the neuromuscular junction characterised by
fluctuating, fatigable weakness of ocular, bulbar, limb and/or respiratory muscles, caused by antibodies
directed against the postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor (AChR) or related proteins such as muscle-specific
tyrosine kinase (MuSK) or lipoprotein receptor-related protein 4 (LRP4).

MGFA clinical classification: the Myasthenia Gravis Foundation of America classification of disease
severity (Classes I to V), used throughout this guideline as the primary severity metric for coverage decisions.

Table 1: MGFA clinical classification of myasthenia gravis severity

Class Description
Class I Ocular weakness only (ptosis and/or diplopia), with or without eyelid closure weakness; all other
muscle strength normal
Class II Mild weakness of muscles other than ocular. IIa predominantly limb or axial; IIb predominantly
oropharyngeal or respiratory
Class III Moderate weakness of muscles other than ocular. IIIa predominantly limb or axial; IIIb
predominantly oropharyngeal or respiratory
Class IV Severe weakness of muscles other than ocular. IVa predominantly limb or axial; IVb
predominantly oropharyngeal or respiratory (may include feeding tube without intubation)
Class V Intubation, with or without mechanical ventilation, except when used in routine postoperative
management


Intravenous immune globulin (IVIG): pooled human immunoglobulin G obtained from thousands of
donors, used as a rapid-acting immunomodulatory therapy in MG. Clinical effect is usually seen within one
week and the benefit generally lasts three to six weeks.

Scope:
This guideline governs the medical necessity and pre-authorisation of IVIG for children, adolescents and
adults with a confirmed diagnosis of myasthenia gravis, in line with the CHI.

This guideline does NOT cover:
• Mild flares (isolated ptosis or diplopia, mild facial or limb weakness) that are manageable by adjusting
pyridostigmine and/or the corticosteroid dose.
• Concurrent or immediately sequential use of IVIG and plasma exchange for the same episode, which
provides no additional benefit.
• IVIG used as first-line chronic immunotherapy in stable, well-controlled disease, or in place of a
corticosteroid and steroid-sparing agent in a patient who has no contraindication or intolerance to them.
• Continuation of chronic IVIG beyond two treatment cycles in the absence of a documented objective
clinical response.
• Concurrent chronic IVIG together with an FcRn inhibitor, a complement C5 inhibitor or rituximab for
the same patient, which constitutes therapeutic duplication.
• Repeat courses requested on a fixed schedule without documentation of recurrent exacerbation or of
maintained objective benefit.
• MuSK-antibody positive MG, where plasma exchange and rituximab are the preferred options. IVIG
remains covered for crisis and acute exacerbation but is not the preferred chronic therapy in MuSK
disease.

Policy:

Eligibility and Coverage Criteria:
IVIG is covered for a patient with an established diagnosis of MG when criterion A is met, AND at least one
of criteria B, C, D or E is met:

A: Confirmed diagnosis of MG documented by a neurologist, supported by:
o Positive serum AChR antibody; or
o If AChR antibody is negative, a positive MuSK antibody; or
o a positive antibody result on a cell-based assay (for example clustered AChR or LRP4); or
o In seronegative patients, a decremental response on repetitive nerve stimulation and/or increased
jitter on single-fibre electromyography, with a compatible clinical picture.
B: Myasthenic crisis — respiratory failure or severe bulbar weakness requiring ventilatory support or airway
protection.
C: Acute exacerbation requiring a change in therapy — Significant worsening such as increasing dysphagia,
dyspnoea or worsening bulbar or limb weakness, corresponding to MGFA class IIIb or higher, or an MG-
ADL increase of at least 3 points from the patient’s stable baseline, or a QMG score above 10.5.
D: Bridge therapy — To obtain rapid symptom control while a slower-acting immunotherapy (corticosteroid,
steroid-sparing agent or rituximab) takes effect.
E: Refractory MG (chronic IVIG) — that remains inadequately controlled on optimised pyridostigmine and
an adequate corticosteroid regimen, or where corticosteroid escalation is contraindicated or not tolerated.

Continuation and Re-authorisation:
- Acute courses — are re-authorised for each documented recurrent exacerbation.

- Chronic IVIG — is authorised initially for six months (approximately four to six cycles).

- Re-authorisation of chronic IVIG — requires a documented improvement of at least 2 points on the
MG-ADL or 3 points on the QMG compared with the pre-treatment baseline, together with evidence of
an attempted corticosteroid taper or infusion interval extension. Where these are met, a further twelve
months may be authorised.

Documentation Requirements:
1. Neurologist note confirming the diagnosis and current severity/exacerbation.
2. Antibody status and/or electrodiagnostic report.
3. Current weight (kg) for dose calculation.
4. Baseline renal function.
5. ICD-10 and SBS codes coded to the highest level of specificity and accuracy.

Approved Dosing:


Parameter Detail
Acute / rescue dose 2 g/kg per course, usually 0.4 g/kg/day over 2 to 5 days
Administration Spread over more days in renal disease, congestive heart failure, thrombotic
risk or older adults
Chronic / maintenance dose 1 to 2 g/kg every 4 to 6 weeks, individualised to the lowest effective dose
Onset of effect Usually within 1 week
Duration of benefit Approximately 3 to 6 weeks
Initial authorisation (chronic) 6 months; continuation requires MG-ADL improvement of at least 2 points

covered. Letters A to E refer to the eligibility criteria in the Policy section.

documents.title: Inflammatory Bowel Disease – Biologic Therapy
pages:
Guideline: Clinical indications for biologics in IBD

Definition:
• Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) comprises ulcerative colitis (UC) and Crohn’s disease (CD), chronic immune-
mediated disorders of the gastrointestinal tract.
• Since there are no curative medical therapies, IBD is a non-communicable, chronic disease that needs lifelong
treatment in the vast majority of cases.
• Treatment may follow a traditional step-up approach, starting with mesalazine (UC only), followed by
immunomodulators, then biologics; however, early biologic therapy may be appropriate in selected high-risk
patients.


• Biologic therapies used for moderate-to-severe IBD include:
o Anti-TNF agents: infliximab, adalimumab, golimumab (UC only), certolizumab (CD only).
o Anti-integrin therapy: vedolizumab.
o Anti-IL-12/23 therapy: ustekinumab (Stelara).
o Anti-IL-23 therapy: risankizumab (CD only), mirikizumab (UC only).


Scope:
This This guideline applies to insurance coverage decisions for biologic therapy in patients with confirmed moderate-
to-severe inflammatory bowel disease.

This guideline does NOTcover:
- Symptoms without confirmed IBD diagnosis.
- Mild disease without poor prognostic factors: Biologic therapy for mild, non-progressive UC or CD that has not
failed, and does not warrant bypassing, conventional therapy is not covered under this guideline.
- Insufficient documentation: no disease severity, objective inflammation, prior treatment history, or treatment
response.


Policy:
Requirements for coverage:

• Confirmed diagnosis: UC or CD must be supported by endoscopy, histology, radiology, or specialist
documentation.
• Disease severity: Evidence must show moderate-to-severe disease, based on symptoms, endoscopy, biomarkers,
or hospitalization for acute severe disease.
• Treatment history: Submission must show prior conventional therapy and response/failure/intolerance, or poor
prognostic factors justifying upfront advanced therapy.

Approval Criteria:
1. Moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis:

Biologic therapy may be approved when either of the following ulcerative colitis pathways is met:

1. Mayo Score (Outpatient Pathway)

Biologic therapy may be approved for patients with moderate-to-severe active ulcerative colitis in the
outpatient setting if any of the following apply:

a. Total Mayo score of 6–12, with Mayo Endoscopic Subscore (MES) of 2 or 3.

b. Mild clinical symptoms but objective evidence of significant inflammatory burden and/or poor prognostic
features.

Any of the following features may predict a higher risk for long term sequelae (eg, colectomy):
• Extensive colitis.
• Deep colonic ulcers.
• Age <40 years.
• Elevated CRP and/or ESR.
• Glucocorticoid requirement to maintain remission or Non-response or intolerance to an adequate trial
• History of hospitalization for UC .
• Co-existing infection (Clostridioidesdifficileinfection or cytomegalovirus infection)


c. Glucocorticoid-dependent or refractory disease.

o Inability to taper corticosteroids without symptom recurrence, or failure to respond to an adequate corticosteroid
course.

1.2. Acute Severe Ulcerative Colitis (ASUC)


Biologic therapy may be approved for patients with acute severe ulcerative colitis (ASUC) when the patient
meets Truelove and Witts criteria as:

≥6 bloody bowel movements per day PLUS at least ONE of the following systemic toxicity features (all four are not
required simultaneously):
• Fever > 37.8°C (100°F)
• Tachycardia > 90 beats per minute
• Anemia: Hemoglobin < 10.5 g/dL
• Elevated ESR > 30 mm/hr or elevated CRP (CRP ≥12 mg/L has been suggested as a sensitive cut-off for
determining UC severity.)

KeyPearl:
Repeat endoscopy is not mandatory before biologic approval when ulcerative colitis and prior active endoscopic disease
have already been documented. Previous endoscopic findings may be accepted in conjunction with current clinical and
objective evidence of active inflammation (e.g., fecal calprotectin and/or CRP). Repeat endoscopy should be requested
when disease activity is uncertain, available documentation is inadequate, or endoscopic reassessment is clinically
indicated.


2. Moderate-to-severe Crohn’s disease

Moderate-to-severe Crohn’s disease may be defined by validated disease activity scores and/or high-risk features,
with objective evidence of active inflammation.

2.1: As per Clinical scoring systems
Clinical scoring systems include the Crohn's Disease Activity Index (CDAI) and the Harvey-Bradshaw Index (HBI).

CDAI:
- 220–450: moderate disease
- >450: severe disease
Calculator: https://www.mdcalc.com/calc/3318/crohns-disease-activity-index-cdai

HBI:
- 8-16: moderate activity
- >16 indicates severe activity.
Calculator: https://www.mdcalc.com/calc/10069/harvey-bradshaw-index-hbi-crohns-disease

The HBI is a simplified version of the CDAI to collect clinical data related to CD.

The index includes five parameters:
1. Patient well-being for the previous day (very well = 0, slightly below par = 1, poor = 2, very poor = 3, terrible = 4)
2. Abdominal pain for the previous day (none = 0, mild = 1, moderate = 2, severe = 3)
3. Number of liquid or soft stools for the previous day
4. Abdominal mass (none = 0, dubious = 1, definite = 2, definite and tender = 3)
5. Complications (none = 0, yes = 1 point for each: arthralgia, uveitis, erythema nodosum, aphthous ulcer, pyoderma
gangrenosum, anal fissures, appearance of a new fistula, abscess)


2.1: High-risk features (moderate to severe Crohn)

• Diagnosis at a younger age (<30 years)

• History of active or recent tobacco use

• Elevated C-reactive protein and/or fecal calprotectin levels

• Deep ulcers on colonoscopy

• Long segments of small and/or large bowel involvement

• Perianal disease

• Extra-intestinal manifestations

• History of bowel resections

• Patients who have not responded to glucocorticoids (ie, refractory) or who relapse after achieving clinical
remission following induction therapy with glucocorticoids
