documents.title: Nerve Conduction Studies and Electromyography
pages:
Comprehensive EMG/NCS Medical Necessity Guideline
Region: Saudi Arabia
Language: English
Version: 1.0



Purpose of this Document
evidence-based decisions regarding approval or rejection of requests for Nerve Conduction
Studies (NCS) and Electromyography (EMG). It summarizes the clinical role of these tests,
defines appropriate and inappropriate indications, and offers practical decision tools,
examples, and checklists tailored to the workflow of an insurance medical department.
Although the primary focus is on neurology requests, many of the principles also apply to
requests from orthopedics, neurosurgery, physical medicine and rehabilitation, and other
specialties.


1. Background and General Principles
NCS and EMG are specialized neurophysiologic tests used to evaluate the function of
peripheral nerves, nerve roots, neuromuscular junctions, and muscles. They provide
objective information that can confirm or refute a suspected diagnosis, characterize the
severity and distribution of a disorder, and help guide treatment decisions. However, these
tests are resource-intensive and should be reserved for situations in which the results are
likely to influence patient management.

From the payer perspective, it is crucial to ensure that EMG/NCS are used appropriately.
Overuse leads to increased costs without meaningful benefit, while underuse may delay
diagnosis of significant neurologic conditions. The key concept of medical necessity is
therefore central to this guideline. A test is medically necessary when:
• The clinical evaluation alone is insufficient to confirm or exclude an important suspected
diagnosis; and
• The result of the test will reasonably be expected to change management, such as
confirming a diagnosis, ruling out serious disease, guiding surgical decisions, or altering
medication or rehabilitation plans.


2. Overview of NCS and EMG
Nerve Conduction Studies (NCS) measure how quickly and strongly electrical signals travel
along peripheral nerves. These tests assess large myelinated fibers and are particularly
useful for detecting focal entrapment neuropathies such as carpal tunnel syndrome,

generalized polyneuropathies such as diabetic neuropathy, and focal mononeuropathies
such as radial or peroneal nerve palsies.

Electromyography (EMG) involves inserting a fine needle electrode into selected muscles to
assess their electrical activity at rest and during voluntary contraction. EMG is especially
important for evaluating radiculopathies, plexopathies, motor neuron disease (such as
amyotrophic lateral sclerosis), and myopathic processes. In clinical practice, NCS and EMG
are frequently performed together as a combined study, and this guideline treats them as a
unified service unless otherwise specified.


3. General Indications by Symptom Category
Medical reviewers will frequently see EMG/NCS requests framed around one or more
symptoms: numbness, tingling, pain, weakness, gait disturbance, or abnormal movements.
The presence, pattern, and progression of these symptoms, combined with the neurological
examination, are critical in determining whether testing is warranted.

3.1 Numbness and Tingling (Paresthesia)
EMG/NCS may be indicated when numbness or tingling:
• Follows a clear peripheral nerve or dermatomal distribution (for example, median nerve
involvement in the first three digits of the hand);
• Has persisted for at least 4–6 weeks despite conservative measures;
• Is associated with objective sensory loss on examination or functional impairment such as
dropping objects or difficulty with fine motor tasks;
• Is unilateral or markedly asymmetric, raising concern for focal entrapment or
radiculopathy; or
• Occurs in a patient with diabetes or other systemic risk factors where there is concern for
superimposed focal neuropathy or atypical neuropathy.

Testing is usually not indicated when paresthesia is diffuse, intermittent, clearly related to
anxiety or hyperventilation, or when there is a completely normal neurologic examination
and no impact on function.


3.2 Weakness
Objective weakness is one of the strongest indications for EMG/NCS. Reviewers should look
for documentation that demonstrates true loss of strength rather than fatigue or subjective
heaviness. EMG/NCS are typically appropriate when there is:
• Focal limb weakness suggestive of a mononeuropathy or radiculopathy (for example, foot
drop, wrist drop, difficulty with ankle dorsiflexion, or loss of shoulder abduction);
• Progressive or unexplained proximal weakness raising concern for myopathy or
neuromuscular junction disease;
• Asymmetrical weakness in a patient with known polyneuropathy where an additional
focal lesion is suspected; or

• Rapidly progressive weakness affecting respiratory or bulbar muscles, which may require
urgent evaluation.

EMG/NCS are usually not indicated when the only complaint is generalized fatigue, mild
subjective weakness without any abnormal findings on examination, or weakness clearly
explained by non-neurologic conditions such as severe pain, joint disease, or
deconditioning.


3.3 Pain
Pain alone is a weak indication for EMG/NCS. These tests should not be used as a general
screening tool for chronic pain. However, they may be appropriate when pain is
accompanied by neurological signs or follows a specific neurologic pattern. EMG/NCS may
be approved when:
• There is radicular pain (neck or back pain radiating down an arm or leg) lasting more than
6 weeks despite conservative therapy, especially when accompanied by weakness, reflex
asymmetry, or dermatomal sensory loss;
• There is focal limb pain in a distribution that strongly suggests entrapment neuropathy; or
• There is suspicion of complex regional pain syndrome or nerve injury following trauma or
surgery and the result will change management.

EMG/NCS should generally be rejected for nonspecific low back pain, fibromyalgia,
mechanical joint pain, and other pain syndromes without evidence of neurologic
involvement.


4. Indications by Disease Category
Reviewers may also encounter EMG/NCS requests linked to specific suspected or
established diagnoses. The following subsections outline conditions where testing is
typically appropriate, conditionally appropriate, or usually not necessary.

4.1 Entrapment Neuropathies
Common examples include carpal tunnel syndrome, ulnar neuropathy at the elbow,
peroneal neuropathy at the fibular head, and tarsal tunnel syndrome. EMG/NCS are usually
indicated when:
• There is a consistent history of focal numbness, tingling, or weakness in the distribution of
a specific nerve;
• Symptoms have persisted beyond 4–6 weeks or have not responded to initial conservative
treatment such as splinting or activity modification; and
• Surgical decompression is being considered and objective confirmation is required.

4.2 Radiculopathies
In suspected cervical or lumbar radiculopathy, EMG/NCS can support the diagnosis and
help differentiate radiculopathy from peripheral neuropathy or plexopathy. Appropriate

indications include:
• Radiating limb pain in a dermatomal pattern lasting more than 6 weeks;
• Weakness in muscles innervated by the suspected root; and
• Abnormal reflexes or sensory loss consistent with the suspected root level.

If high-quality imaging (such as MRI) and the clinical picture already clearly support the
diagnosis and no change in management is expected based on EMG findings, testing may be
unnecessary.


4.3 Polyneuropathies
For patients with suspected generalized peripheral neuropathy, EMG/NCS are often the
most informative tests. They help distinguish axonal from demyelinating processes and
guide further investigations. Testing is generally appropriate when:
• There is length-dependent sensory loss, starting in the feet and potentially progressing to
the hands;
• Reflexes are reduced or absent distally;
• There is weakness in distal muscles; or
• There is concern for rapidly progressive or inflammatory neuropathy.

4.4 Myopathies
EMG is a valuable tool in the evaluation of primary muscle disease. Approval may be
appropriate for patients with:
• Symmetric proximal weakness (difficulty climbing stairs, rising from a chair, or lifting
arms overhead);
• Elevated creatine kinase or other evidence of muscle involvement; and
• Family history or clinical suspicion of inherited myopathy or inflammatory myositis.


4.5 Motor Neuron Disease and ALS
When clinicians suspect amyotrophic lateral sclerosis or another motor neuron disease,
EMG is essential for confirming the diagnosis and excluding mimics. EMG/NCS should be
approved in the presence of:
• Progressive weakness affecting multiple regions (bulbar, cervical, thoracic, lumbosacral);
• Upper and lower motor neuron signs on examination; or
• Fasciculations, muscle atrophy, and unexplained weight loss.


5. Situations Where EMG/NCS Are Usually Not Indicated
Medical reviewers should feel confident rejecting EMG/NCS requests when the clinical
scenario does not support neurologic testing or when results will not change management.
Common low-value indications include:
• Diffuse musculoskeletal pain without neurologic deficits;
• Fibromyalgia and other centralized pain syndromes;

• Chronic low back pain without radiation, sensory changes, or weakness;
• Subjective numbness or tingling with completely normal neurological examination and no
functional limitation;
• Follow-up of a stable, well-characterized neuropathy without any change in symptoms;
• Repeat EMG/NCS within 6 months of a previous study unless there is clear documentation
of new or rapidly progressive deficits.


6. Required Documentation for Approval
To approve EMG/NCS, reviewers should expect a minimum standard of documentation in
the request. The following elements are strongly recommended:
• A clear statement of the main symptom(s) and duration (for example, 'right hand
numbness for 3 months' or 'progressive left foot drop over 6 weeks');
• Relevant neurological examination findings, including muscle strength grades, sensory
changes, reflex findings, and presence of atrophy or fasciculations;
• Clinical differential diagnosis or working diagnosis (for example, 'suspected L5
radiculopathy' or 'rule out carpal tunnel syndrome versus cervical radiculopathy');
• Description of any prior investigations that relate to the request, such as MRI of the spine
or brain, and whether the results are concordant or discordant with the clinical findings;
• Documentation of previous conservative management and response (physiotherapy,
splinting, medications);
• The specialty of the requesting physician, with neurology, neurosurgery, or physical
medicine and rehabilitation typically providing the most detailed neurodiagnostic rationale.


7. Stepwise Reviewer Decision Algorithm
A simple, repeatable approach can help reviewers reach consistent decisions. The following
algorithm can be applied to most EMG/NCS requests:

Step 1 – Confirm the primary symptom and its duration.
• If symptoms have lasted less than 4–6 weeks and there are no red flags, consider
suggesting continued conservative management before testing.

Step 2 – Look for objective neurological findings.
• Approvals should generally require at least one documented abnormal neurological sign
(weakness, sensory loss, reflex change, atrophy, or fasciculations).

Step 3 – Assess whether the clinical picture suggests a focal or generalized neurologic
problem.
• Focal deficits (single nerve or root distribution) or clear length-dependent neuropathy are
more likely to benefit from testing.

Step 4 – Ask whether EMG/NCS will change management.
• If the treating physician clearly explains that results will guide surgery, confirm diagnosis,

or differentiate between two competing conditions, testing is more likely to be justified.

Step 5 – Check for recent prior EMG/NCS.
• Avoid approving repeat testing within 6 months unless new deficits or major clinical
changes are documented.


8. High-Priority and Automatically Approved Scenarios
Certain clinical scenarios carry a high risk of serious neurologic disease and should
generally be approved without delay:
• New-onset foot drop or wrist drop with supporting examination findings;
• Rapidly progressive limb weakness over days to weeks;
• Suspected Guillain–Barré syndrome (acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy);
• Suspected motor neuron disease (ALS) with appropriate clinical features;
• Severe radicular symptoms with objective deficits where surgery is being considered;
• Suspected neuromuscular junction disorders causing fatigable weakness or respiratory
compromise.


9. Case-Based Examples for Reviewers
Case 1 – Appropriate Request
A 52-year-old woman with diabetes presents with progressive numbness and tingling in the
first three digits of her right hand for 4 months. She reports dropping objects and nocturnal
symptoms. Examination reveals reduced sensation in the median nerve distribution and
mild weakness of thumb abduction. The neurologist requests EMG/NCS to confirm carpal
tunnel syndrome and assess severity before considering surgery. This is an appropriate
indication and should be approved.

Case 2 – Inappropriate Request
A 40-year-old man presents with diffuse back pain for 2 years. There is no radiation of pain,
no numbness or weakness, and neurological examination is normal. The physician requests
EMG/NCS 'to rule out nerve damage.' There is no clear neurologic indication, and results are
unlikely to change management. This request should be rejected.

Case 3 – Borderline Request
A 60-year-old woman reports intermittent tingling in both hands for 2 weeks, worse at
night. Neurological examination is normal. The physician requests EMG/NCS immediately.
In this scenario, conservative treatment with wrist splints and observation is reasonable
before testing. Reviewers may reasonably reject or defer approval pending a trial of
conservative management and reassessment if symptoms persist or progress.

10. Reviewer Checklist
Before approving EMG/NCS, reviewers should answer 'yes' to most of the following
questions:
• Is there a clearly stated clinical question or suspected diagnosis?
• Are there documented objective neurologic findings?
• Have symptoms persisted for at least 4–6 weeks (except in urgent cases)?
• Is the condition one in which EMG/NCS are known to be helpful (for example, entrapment
neuropathy, radiculopathy, polyneuropathy, myopathy, motor neuron disease)?
• Is it likely that test results will change management?
• Has unnecessary repeat testing been avoided?


EMG and NCS are valuable diagnostic tools when used in the right clinical context. For
low-value or unnecessary studies. By focusing on symptom duration, objective neurologic
findings, appropriate disease categories, and a clear link between test results and
management decisions, reviewers can make balanced, consistent, and defensible
determinations.

This guideline is intended to be a living document. As new evidence emerges and as local
practice patterns evolve, it may be updated or expanded. Feedback from reviewers and
clinicians is encouraged to improve clarity, applicability, and ease of use in daily decision-
making.

Guideline:

Precocious Puberty
Definitions:

Precocious puberty: Onset of secondary sexual characteristics before age 8 years in girls (breast development,
Tanner B2) or before age 9 years in boys (testicular volume ≥4 mL), confirmed on physical examination.
Central precocious puberty (CPP): GnRH-dependent ("true") precocious puberty caused by premature activation
of the hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal (HPG) axis resulting in progressive pubertal development with pubertal
gonadotropin secretion. Could be idiopathic or secondary to central nervous system pathology.
Peripheral precocious puberty (PPP): GnRH-independent ("pseudo-") precocious puberty resulting from an
autonomous source of sex steroids (ovarian, testicular, adrenal, exogenous, or hCG-secreting tumor) with suppressed
basal and stimulated gonadotropins.
Progressive puberty: Documented advancement of pubertal (Tanner) staging, accelerated linear growth velocity,
and/or bone age advancement on serial assessment. Rapid progression is defined as advancement to Tanner B3
within 6 months of the onset of thelarche.
Non-progressive premature thelarche: Isolated, typically stable or slowly regressing breast development, most
common under age 3 years, without other pubertal signs, without significant growth acceleration, and without
significant bone age advancement.
Premature adrenarche: Isolated early appearance of pubic and/or axillary hair and adult-type body odor due to
early adrenal androgen production, without breast development (girls) or testicular enlargement (boys), and without
significant growth acceleration.
Bone age advancement: Skeletal (bone) age, assessed by the Greulich-Pyle atlas on a left hand-wrist radiograph,
significantly greater than chronological age — a key indicator of sex-steroid exposure and a determinant of predicted
adult height.
Tanner staging: Standardized five-stage classification (Tanner I–V) of breast development and pubic hair in girls,
and genital development and pubic hair in boys, used to document pubertal onset and progression.


Scope:

Included:
• Children referred for evaluation of suspected precocious puberty.
• Confirmed central precocious puberty (CPP).
• Confirmed peripheral precocious puberty (PPP).
• Monitoring of approved GnRH-agonist therapy and continuation/discontinuation decisions.

Excluded:
• Isolated, non-progressive premature thelarche.
• Isolated premature adrenarche.
• Normal pubertal timing variants (including constitutional/familial early normal puberty).
• Delayed puberty.
• Adult endocrine disorders and adult reproductive endocrinology.

Policy:
• Requirements for coverage
Documentation Requirements:
• Patient age and sex
• Growth chart (height, weight, BMI plotted against age- and sex-specific percentiles).
• Height velocity (cm/year), calculated from at least two measurements 3–6 months apart.
• Pubertal (Tanner) staging, with date of onset and serial findings if available.
Additional requirements for treatment (GnRH agonist or peripheral-precocity therapy) requests:
• Bone-age report (radiograph and interpretation).
• Basal LH (and FSH) results.
• Estradiol (girls) or testosterone (boys).
• GnRH/GnRH-agonist stimulation test result, if performed (required when basal LH is discordant with
clinical picture).
• Details of any previous treatment (agent, dose, duration, response).
• Written recommendation from Pediatric Endocrinologist for pharmacologic treatment.
• For suspected peripheral precocity: relevant imaging (pelvic/testicular ultrasound, adrenal imaging),
adrenal steroid panel, or karyotype as applicable to the suspected etiology.

First: Approve routinely (once diagnostic evaluation is clinically indicated):
• Basal LH, FSH, Estradiol (girls) or testosterone (boys).

Coverage Criteria — Treatment:
GnRH agonist therapy for central precocious puberty:
Treatment is medically necessary when ALL the following are present:
1. Age: Girl < 8 years. Boys < 9 years

2. Evidence of progressive Puberty:
• Advancement in Tanner stage within 3-6 months
• Accelerated height velocity (>6 cm/year)
• Advanced bone age (>2 years above chronological age)
3. Laboratory confirmation:
• Basal LH ≥ pubertal range
Or

4. Pediatric endocrinologist recommendation


Special Consideration: Rapidly Progressive Puberty After the Age Cut-off
For puberty starting at ≥8 years in girls or ≥9 years in boys, GnRH-agonist treatment is not routinely indicated based
on age or rapid progression alone.
Treatment may be considered on an individualized basis when ALL the following are present:
• Rapid pubertal progression: Tanner-stage advancement within 3–6 months and/or accelerated growth
velocity (>6 cm/year).
• Advanced bone age: preferably ≥2 years above chronological age or significant advancement on serial
assessment.
• Compromised height potential: predicted adult height (PAH) below or progressively declining relative
to mid-parental/target height.
• Confirmed central puberty: pubertal basal LH or pubertal response to GnRH/GnRH-agonist stimulation.
• Pediatric Endocrinologist recommendation, documenting the expected benefit of GnRH-agonist
treatment.

Rapid Tanner progression or advanced bone age alone is insufficient for treatment approval.

Do NOT approve GnRH-agonist treatment when:
• Puberty is slowly progressive (ie. no change in Tanner (breast/genital/pubic hair) stage over ≥6 months of
observation) — these children generally reach target adult height without treatment and girls with slow
progression typically experience menarche at a normal age (~11 years) untreated.
• Predicted adult height approximates mid-parental target height — a conservative (no-treatment) approach
is appropriate regardless of chronological age.

Continuation Criteria:
Continued approval requires ALL the following:
• Ongoing Pediatric Endocrinology follow-up, generally every 3–6 months.
• Clinical evidence of pubertal suppression: stabilization or regression of secondary sexual characteristics, no
new progression in Tanner stage.
• Growth velocity normalizing toward pre-pubertal, age-appropriate rate.
• Bone age advancement appropriately slowing on interval imaging.

Monitoring:
Clinical monitoring (every 3-6 months):
• Pubertal development (Tanner stage) and growth velocity. Effective therapy should show cessation of
further breast/testicular development and menses, with declining height velocity.
• Vaginal bleeding (girls): expected transiently within the first weeks of therapy due to estradiol withdrawal;
if it occurs later in treatment, this indicates incomplete suppression or an alternative diagnosis and should
prompt reassessment.

guide dose/interval adjustment), such testing should be approved.

advancement; once this is documented, frequency may be reduced to every 1–2 years.
• Repeat brain MRI only if new CNS signs/symptoms develop; not on a routine interval basis.


Discontinuation Criteria

concordant pubertal timing.

pages:
Guideline: Laboratory Testing for the Diagnosis of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)

Definitions:
Rheumatoid arthritis (RA): a chronic inflammatory arthritis characterised by synovitis that predominantly
affects the small joints of the hands, wrists and feet in a symmetric distribution.

Synovitis: joint inflammation demonstrated on physical examination, or, where the physical examination is
inconclusive, on ultrasonography or magnetic resonance imaging. Joint pain in the absence of synovitis does
not constitute synovitis.

Rheumatoid factor (RF) and anti-citrullinated peptide antibodies (ACPA): the two RA-associated
autoantibodies. ACPA is measured in clinical practice as the anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP)
antibody. A high positive result is a titre above three times the upper limit of normal; a low positive result is
a titre above the upper limit of normal but not exceeding three times that limit.

Acute phase reactants: the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and the C-reactive protein (CRP).

Seronegative RA: RA in which both RF and ACPA are negative. Both are negative at presentation in up to
50 percent of patients and remain negative during follow-up in 20 percent.

Felty syndrome (FS): RA with persistent neutropenia, an absolute neutrophil count (ANC) below
2,000/microL that is not explained by concurrent illness or drug therapy, usually with splenomegaly.



Scope:
This guideline governs the medical necessity and pre-authorisation of laboratory testing performed for the
diagnosis and classification of RA, for the monitoring of RA disease activity, and for the assessment of extra-
articular and comorbid disease in adults.

This guideline does NOT cover:
§ Laboratory testing performed for the safety monitoring of disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, biologic
agents, Janus kinase inhibitors or glucocorticoids, which is governed by the companion guideline on
laboratory monitoring of therapy in rheumatoid arthritis.
§ Juvenile idiopathic arthritis and any patient below 18 years of age.
§ Multi-biomarker disease activity testing, including the Vectra DA score.
§ Anti-mutated citrullinated vimentin (anti-MCV) antibodies, serum 14-3-3eta and anti-carbamylated
protein (anti-CarP) antibodies.
§ Human leukocyte antigen typing and any other genetic or pharmacogenetic testing for the diagnosis of
RA.
§ Serum Krebs von den Lungen-6 (KL-6), matrix metalloproteinases, interferon gamma-induced protein 10,
anti-citrullinated heat shock protein 90 antibodies and leukocyte telomere length.
§ High-sensitivity CRP performed for cardiovascular risk stratification.

Policy:

Serologic Testing for the Diagnosis of RA:

- RF, ACPA and one or both acute phase reactants are covered once where both of the following are met:
§ A: Synovitis is present in at least one joint; AND
§ B: No alternative diagnosis better explains the synovitis.

RF and ACPA are not covered in patients with joint pain in the absence of synovitis, including nonspecific
arthralgia, fibromyalgia and osteoarthritis, and are not covered as a screening test in asymptomatic individuals.

Where a documented RF or ACPA result already exists, a repeat measurement of that antibody is not covered.

- CBC, serum creatinine and aminotransferases are covered once at the time of diagnosis.

- The following non-laboratory investigations are covered as part of the diagnostic assessment:
§ Plain radiographs: of the hands and wrists and an anteroposterior view of both forefeet, once at diagnosis.
§ Ultrasonography: of the affected joints where synovitis cannot be determined on physical examination, or
magnetic resonance imaging where ultrasonography is not available.

Laboratory Monitoring of Disease Activity:

- ESR and/or CRP are covered at each disease assessment, at the following intervals:
§ Every 3 months while disease is active, until the patient is stable in remission or in low disease activity.
§ Every 3 to 6 months once remission or low disease activity is sustained.
§ At any additional visit prompted by a documented disease flare, a change of therapy or a dose increase.

- CBC, serum creatinine and aminotransferases obtained for drug safety monitoring under the companion
guideline are not separately covered as disease-activity tests.

- In patients treated with an interleukin 6 receptor inhibitor or a Janus kinase inhibitor, a normal ESR or CRP
does not establish remission, and a composite disease activity measure that contains no acute phase reactant
is required to document treatment response.

- Repeat plain radiographs, ultrasonography and magnetic resonance imaging are not covered for routine
disease-activity monitoring, and are covered only where there is clinical evidence of disease progression or
the joint examination is equivocal.

Suspected Rheumatoid Arthritis-Associated Interstitial Lung Disease:
- In a patient with RA and respiratory symptoms, abnormal pulmonary function testing or a chest radiograph
suggesting diffuse parenchymal disease, the following are covered:
§ CBC with differential.
§ Serum natriuretic peptide.

- Antinuclear antibodies, anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies, a myositis antibody panel and cryoglobulins
are covered only where purpura, Raynaud phenomenon, skin ulcers or renal disease is documented.

- ESR and CRP are not covered for the evaluation of lung disease.

Suspected Felty Syndrome:
- Where a patient with RA has an ANC below 2,000/microL on at least two occasions and drug-induced
neutropenia has been excluded, the following are covered:
§ CBC with differential white blood cell count.
§ Peripheral blood smear review with immunophenotypic analysis, to exclude large granular lymphocyte
leukaemia.
§ RF and ACPA, where no result is already documented.
§ Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy with immunophenotypic and clonality analysis, where analysis of the
peripheral blood is insufficient to exclude leukaemia.

- Antihistone antibodies, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies and anti-glucose-6-phosphate isomerase
antibodies are not covered for the diagnosis of Felty syndrome, and serum Fc-gamma RIII and granulocyte
colony-stimulating factor concentrations are not covered.

Cardiovascular Risk Assessment:
- A fasting lipid panel comprising total cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein, high-density lipoprotein and
triglycerides is covered as an input to a validated cardiovascular risk calculator, on the same terms as in the
general population.

Documentation Requirements:

§ Treating physician note describing the joints examined and the presence of synovitis, or the
ultrasonographic or magnetic resonance findings relied on.
§ For diagnostic serology, confirmation that no previous RF or ACPA result is available.
§ For disease-activity monitoring, the established diagnosis of RA, the current therapy and the date of the
last covered acute phase reactant.
§ For extra-articular testing, the clinical finding that triggers the test, being the respiratory finding, the
documented ANC or the clinical feature listed above.
§ ICD-10 and SBS codes coded to the highest level of specificity and accuracy.

Guideline: Laboratory Monitoring of Therapy in Rheumatoid Arthritis

Definitions:
Rheumatoid arthritis (RA): a chronic inflammatory arthritis characterised by synovitis that predominantly
affects the small joints of the hands, wrists and feet in a symmetric distribution.

Conventional synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (csDMARD): methotrexate (MTX),
leflunomide (LEF), sulfasalazine (SSZ), hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) and azathioprine (AZA).

Biologic disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (bDMARD): the tumour necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitors
adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab, certolizumab pegol and golimumab; abatacept; rituximab; and the
interleukin 6 (IL-6) receptor inhibitors tocilizumab and sarilumab.

Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor: tofacitinib, baricitinib and upadacitinib.

Pre-treatment screening: laboratory testing obtained before the first dose of an agent to establish safety of
initiation and a baseline for later monitoring.

Scope:
This guideline governs the medical necessity and pre-authorisation of laboratory testing performed for the
safety monitoring of csDMARD, bDMARD, JAK inhibitor and glucocorticoid therapy in adults with RA.

This guideline does NOT cover:
§ Laboratory testing for the diagnosis and classification of RA, for the monitoring of RA disease activity
and for the assessment of extra-articular and comorbid disease, which is governed by the companion
guideline on laboratory testing in rheumatoid arthritis.
§ Juvenile idiopathic arthritis and any patient below 18 years of age.
§ The medicines themselves, which are governed by the pharmacy benefit.
§ Leflunomide and teriflunomide concentrations measured to assess efficacy or adherence.
§ Cytochrome P450 (CYP1A2) and dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH) genotyping before
leflunomide.
§ NAT2, HLA-B*08:01 and HLA-A*31:01 genotyping before sulfasalazine.
§ Red cell 6-thioguanine metabolite levels during azathioprine therapy.
§ B-cell or CD19 counts during rituximab therapy.



Policy:
Laboratory testing listed in this guideline is covered where the patient has an established diagnosis of RA and
is starting, or is established on, the agent concerned. Covered intervals are summarised in Table 1.

General Pre-Treatment Screening:
The following is covered once before the first dose of any csDMARD, bDMARD or JAK inhibitor:
§ CBC.
§ Serum creatinine.
§ Aminotransferases.
§ ESR and CRP.
§ Hepatitis B serology comprising HBsAg, anti-HBs and anti-HBc, and hepatitis C serology.
Repeat general pre-treatment screening is not covered when a subsequent agent is started.

Hepatitis B and hepatitis C serology may be repeated only where a new exposure is documented.

In a patient with serologic evidence of prior hepatitis B infection, an HBV viral load is covered every 6 to 12
months for the duration of therapy.

Additional Pre-Treatment Screening by Agent:
- Before any bDMARD or JAK inhibitor. Latent tuberculosis screening. Repeat screening is covered where
the patient is at increased risk of tuberculosis, has a documented exposure, or has been treated for latent
tuberculosis with potential ongoing exposure. Chest radiograph, where the patient has risk factors for latent
tuberculosis, including where the screening test is negative.

- Before a JAK inhibitor. CBC with differential and platelet count; serum creatinine, blood urea nitrogen
and eGFR; ALT, AST, bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase; a lipid panel; and serum hCG in females of
reproductive age.

- Before an IL-6 receptor inhibitor. CBC with differential and platelet count; ALT, AST, bilirubin and
alkaline phosphatase; a lipid panel; and serum hCG in females of reproductive age.

- Before rituximab. HIV serology and serum immunoglobulins IgG, IgM and IgA. Chest radiograph, where
one has not been obtained within the previous six months.

- Before sulfasalazine. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) assay, where the patient belongs to a
population at high risk of G6PD deficiency, which includes groups originating from the Middle East and the
Mediterranean region.

- Before methotrexate or leflunomide, Chest radiograph.

- Before hydroxychloroquine, Complete ophthalmologic examination, covered within the first year of
therapy.

Conventional Synthetic DMARDs:
- Methotrexate, Leflunomide and Sulfasalazine, a CBC, aminotransferases and serum creatinine are
covered, with serum albumin for methotrexate:
§ Every 2 to 4 weeks for the first 3 months of therapy and after any dose increase.
§ Every 8 to 12 weeks for months 3 to 6.
§ Every 12 weeks thereafter.

- Sulfasalazine, a CBC is additionally covered one week after each dose increase.

- Methotrexate and Leflunomide given in combination, a CBC, serum creatinine, albumin and transaminases
are covered every 2 to 4 weeks for the first 3 months and after any dose increase, every 4 weeks for the next
3 months, then every 3 months.

- Leflunomide, where the ALT rises above twice the upper limit of normal, weekly liver function tests are
covered until the ALT returns to the normal range. Where elimination of teriflunomide is required, two serum
teriflunomide concentrations obtained at least 14 days apart are covered.

- Azathioprine, a CBC and platelet count are covered every 1 to 2 weeks with any change of dose and every
1 to 3 months thereafter, with liver function tests every 3 months.

- Azathioprine, TPMT and NUDT15 testing is covered before treatment only if one of the following applies:
§ A: The baseline absolute lymphocyte count is below 800/microL; or
§ B: The patient is taking allopurinol and there is no alternative to starting azathioprine.
- Hydroxychloroquinen, annual ophthalmologic evaluation for retinal toxicity is covered only. no routine lab
toxicity is covered.

Biologic DMARDs:
- TNF inhibitor, a CBC is covered within one month of starting therapy and every 3 to 6 months thereafter
while the white blood cell count remains stable.

- Abatacept, no scheduled laboratory monitoring is covered.

- IL-6 receptor inhibitor, a CBC with differential and liver function tests comprising ALT, AST, alkaline
phosphatase and bilirubin are covered monthly for the first 3 months of therapy and every 3 months thereafter.
A lipid panel is covered 4 to 8 weeks after starting therapy and every 6 months thereafter.

- Rituximab, a CBC with differential is covered 4 to 6 weeks after each treatment course, and at any time up
to one year after an infusion where a severe infection or unusual severe mouth ulceration or mucositis
develops. Serum immunoglobulins are covered before each retreatment and where a serious or repeated
infection develops.

Where a bDMARD is given together with a csDMARD, the monitoring schedule for that csDMARD
continues in full and is covered in addition to the schedule above.

JAK Inhibitors:
The following are covered:
§ CBC with differential, serum creatinine and liver function tests comprising transaminases, albumin and
bilirubin, monthly for the first 3 months of therapy and every 3 months thereafter.
§ A lipid panel 6 to 8 weeks after starting therapy and every 6 months thereafter.

Where a JAK inhibitor is given together with a csDMARD, the monitoring schedule for that csDMARD
continues in full and is covered in addition to the schedule above.

Glucocorticoids:
For a patient on systemic glucocorticoid therapy, the following are covered:
§ Screening for glucose intolerance and type 2 diabetes, at an increased frequency where the patient is on a
moderate or high dose or on a prolonged course of low-dose therapy.
§ A fasting lipid panel.
§ Latent tuberculosis screening, where the patient is on high-dose therapy.
§ Non-laboratory. Bone mineral density measurement, where a prolonged course or a high dose is
anticipated.
§ Non-laboratory. Periodic ophthalmologic examination, where the patient is on a prolonged course of
moderate or high-dose therapy.

No scheduled CBC, serum creatinine or liver panel is covered for glucocorticoid therapy alone.

Documentation Requirements:
§ Treating physician note stating the diagnosis of RA, the agent, the dose and the date of initiation.
§ For pre-treatment screening, confirmation that the agent has not previously been given and that the
screening tests have not already been performed.
§ For on-treatment monitoring, the date of the last covered panel for that agent and any dose increase since
that date.
§ For any concurrent csDMARD, the name of that agent and its dose.

Guideline: Skin and soft tissue Infection


Definition:
Skin and soft tissue infection management centers on early recognition and standardized treatment of both
purulent infections (furuncle, carbuncle, paronychia, abscess) and non-purulent infections (cellulitis,
erysipelas), with a primary focus on rapid source control, preventing escalation to deeper or systemic
involvement, and guiding consistent, evidence-based care across ER and outpatient settings.
Scope:
This guideline covers the diagnosis and management of skin and cutaneous infection, both Purulent & Non-
Purulent.
Policy:

• Diagnosis:
o The diagnosis of skin infection is usually based on clinical diagnosis.
o Laboratory testing is not required for patients with uncomplicated infection in the absence of
comorbidities or complications.
▪ Blood tests (WBC, CRP): helpful in evaluating systemic response or monitoring progression in
moderate to severe infections.
o Imaging:
▪ Ultrasound may help to assess the presence of abscess and extent
▪ Radiographic evaluation may be warranted in patients with underlying immunosuppression,
diabetes mellitus, venous insufficiency, or lymphedema and in patients with persistent systemic
symptoms.
▪ CT scan: indicated if deep space infection, gas in soft tissues, or necrotizing fasciitis is suspected

• Management:

Purulent skin and soft tissue infections:

Mild: without systemic signs of infection
Moderate:
▪ Systemic signs of infection such as temperature higher than 38ºC, heart rate higher than 90 beats/minute,
respiratory rate higher than 24 breaths/ minute, or WBC higher than 12 x 103 cells/mm3.
▪ Patient with comorbidities

Severe:
▪ Systemic signs of infection such as temperature higher than 38ºC, heart rate higher than 90 beats/minute,
respiratory rate higher than 24 breaths/ minute, or WBC higher than 12 x 103 cells/mm.
▪ Immunocompromise
▪ Organ dysfunction (septic shock)
▪ Systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS).
▪ Clinical signs of deeper infection
▪ Infection that fails to improve with incision and drainage plus oral antibiotics.

▪ Incision and drainage are indicated for all cases
o I&D for common cutaneous abscess should be done under Local anesthesia in emergency
or outpatient setting.
o Situations where cutaneous abscess may require drainage under General anesthesia:
▪ Pediatric age group.
▪ Perirectal abscesses.
▪ Anterior and lateral neck abscesses potentially arising from congenital cysts (eg, thyroglossal
duct cysts, branchial cyst, cystic hygroma).
▪ Abscesses adjacent to vital nerves or blood vessels (eg, facial nerve, carotid artery, femoral
artery).
▪ Breast abscesses, particularly those near the areola and nipple.
▪ Large abscesses (>5 cm by palpation or ultrasound).
▪ Recurrent and multiple interconnected abscesses.

Non-purulent Skin and Soft Tissue Infections (Necrotizing
infection/Cellulitis/Erysipelas)

Mild: without systemic signs of infection
Moderate:
▪ Systemic signs of infection such as temperature higher than 38ºC, heart rate higher than 90 beats/minute,
respiratory rate higher than 24 breaths/ minute, or WBC higher than 12 x 103 cells/mm3
Severe:
▪ For patients whose cellulitis is associated with penetrating trauma, evidence of MRSA infection elsewhere, nasal
colonization with MRSA, injection drug use, or SIRS
